extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, in-house counsel, examiners and innovators seeking cross-jurisdictional guidance on inventive step/obviousness
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative summary of how different patent jurisdictions assess inventive step/non-obviousness, including the legal tests, evidentiary practices, and policy considerations used by the US, EPO, China, and India.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive Step / Non-Obviousness (general / TRIPS)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be more than novel — it must involve an inventive step (non-obviousness) and be capable of industrial application. This notion is reflected in Article 27 of the TRIPS Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive step filters out 'incremental advances' and ensures patents reward authentic knowledge-based inventions rather than frivolous tweaks. The article frames this as a universal goal, though national implementation varies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person Having Ordinary Skill in the Art (PHOSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment asks whether the invention would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHOSITA is assumed to possess average expertise and practical knowledge in the relevant field; this hypothetical standard anchors objectivity and helps avoid hindsight. Jurisdictions may characterize the skill level differently in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. §103 — U.S. statutory non-obviousness baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. law provides that a patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art would have made the claimed invention obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory baseline is interpreted through case law (Graham, KSR) and supplemented by evidentiary practices like objective indicia/secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor — scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the Graham factors: determine the scope and content of the prior art relevant to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate identification of relevant prior art is the first analytical step in the U.S. obviousness inquiry; it informs subsequent comparison to the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor — differences between the prior art and the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claimed invention as a whole to the prior art to identify differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comparison isolates what the claim adds over the prior art and is essential to evaluating whether those differences would have been obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor — level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the level of skill in the relevant art (ties closely to PHOSITA) as one of the Graham factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defined skill level affects whether a variation would be considered routine or inventive; evidence and expert testimony commonly inform this assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factor — secondary considerations / objective indicia of non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations include commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and unexpected results as objective signs that an invention was not obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In U.S. practice these factors are not optional: if present they must be evaluated and can tip the obviousness analysis. Applicants often rely on them to bolster non-obviousness arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR common-sense approach (U.S. Supreme Court)
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR International Co. v. Teleflex endorsed a flexible, common-sense approach to obviousness and moved away from a rigid requirement for a formal teaching-suggestion-motivation (TSM) in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under KSR, predictable variations using known techniques can render claims obvious; examiners and courts may consider ordinary creativity and common sense in finding obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: TSM Test (teaching-suggestion-motivation) — prior rigid U.S. approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously, the TSM test required an identifiable teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to combine elements; KSR criticized its rigidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats TSM as a former strict test and indicates its narrowing after KSR as an anti-pattern to overly formalistic obviousness assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO Problem–Solution Approach — identify the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage 1 of the EPO problem-solution approach: identify the closest prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting the proper 'closest' prior art anchors the EPO's structured analysis and is critical to minimizing hindsight bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO Problem–Solution Approach — determine distinguishing aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage 2: determine the features that distinguish the claimed invention from the closest prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This step isolates the technical contribution over the prior art that will be analyzed for inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO Problem–Solution Approach — identify the technical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage 3: identify the technical effect resulting from the distinguishing features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing a technical effect links claim features to concrete improvements and supports formulation of the objective technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO Problem–Solution Approach — define the objective technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage 4: formulate the objective technical problem to be solved in light of the distinguishing features and technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem formulation must be objective (not based on hindsight); it frames what a skilled person would seek to solve and guides the obviousness test.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO Problem–Solution Approach — evaluate obviousness without hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage 5: decide whether, in view of the closest prior art and without using hindsight, the claimed invention would have been obvious to a skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This final evaluation is designed to minimize hindsight bias and to focus on the technical contribution rather than ex post rationalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPO distinction — patentable technical solutions vs abstract ideas/business methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO distinguishes patentable technical solutions from unpatentable abstract ideas or business methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must demonstrate a technical contribution/effect to be patentable under Article 56 EPC; purely abstract or business-method claims are typically excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: China — substantive distinguishing features and notable progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Chinese law requires an invention to exhibit substantive distinguishing features and notable progress over prior art to satisfy inventiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CNIPA emphasizes concrete technical advancement; routine extensions of known methods are liable to be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: China (CNIPA) — unexpected technical effect
rubrics_metrics.description: CNIPA Guidelines state an invention is non-obvious if it demonstrates an 'unexpected technical effect' beyond what prior art would predict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrating an unexpected technical effect (e.g., via experimental results) is especially important in complex fields like AI and pharmaceuticals. The article cites denials (e.g., brain-controlled robotic limbs) where lack of clear performance enhancement data led to rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: China — hybrid EPO + Graham approach and evidentiary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: China uses a hybrid model influenced by both the EPO problem–solution approach and the U.S. Graham factors, and it may incorporate flexible evidentiary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNIPA practice can include both technical-advancement analysis and consideration of experimental/market evidence or secondary indicia when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: India — statutory inventive step: technical advancement or economic significance (Section 2(1)(ja))
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian law defines inventive step as involving technical advancement as compared to existing knowledge or having economic significance or both, making the invention not obvious to a skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory formulation explicitly allows economic significance (in addition to technical advancement) to inform inventive-step assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: India — flexible mixed approach and anti-evergreening policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indian Patent Office and courts apply a flexible mixed approach (drawing on EPO and Graham factors) and maintain a cautious stance to prevent 'evergreening', particularly in pharmaceuticals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indian jurisprudence (e.g., Novartis, Roche decisions) illustrates stricter scrutiny for marginal improvements and emphasizes substantial technical advancement over mere novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimizing hindsight bias / framing objective technical problem
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurrent criterion across jurisdictions (emphasized by the EPO) is avoiding hindsight and ensuring the inventive-step enquiry is framed objectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured methods (like the problem–solution approach) and careful selection of closest prior art are techniques to limit hindsight-driven analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary burdens and treatment of post-filing data
rubrics_metrics.description: Jurisdictions differ in evidentiary burdens and the permissibility/weight of post-filing experimental or market data in inventive-step assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that fields with rapid development (AI, pharma, BCIs) raise particular evidentiary issues; CNIPA may accept experimental results, U.S. considers objective indicia, and admissibility/treatment varies by office/court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonization challenges — policy and socio-economic considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in statutory language, interpretive doctrines, and socio-economic policy goals (e.g., public health in India vs. market orientation in the U.S.) create difficulties in harmonizing inventive-step standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These divergences affect thresholds, evidentiary expectations and procedural frameworks, complicating cross-border patent strategy and technology transfer.
